title: cross-arch-token-window-degradation-case-study
content:
Summary:

This note collects an experiment-driven investigation into a recurrent performance degradation we saw as token window grows beyond ~32k in production shapes for three architecture families: Llama-style dense decoders, Mistral-style transformer blocks with fused attention, and Qwen-style larger-context optimizations. We also exercised an MoE prototype routing layer (sparse experts) to observe interaction effects between routing imbalance, per-expert queuing, and long-context KV behavior. The objective was to identify dominant bottlenecks across architectures and produce a short playbook of mitigations for serving.

Context and symptoms observed:
- Production: tail latency (p95/p99) spikes and occasional soft OOMs when clients send single requests with very long histories (>= 32k tokens).
- Patterns: dense models show steadily rising per-token time; Mistral shows steeper slope past 48k where certain attention kernels lose throughput; Qwen shows non-monotonic spikes tied to KV cache lifecycle. MoE workloads show high variance and tail amplification when a few requests route heavily to a subset of experts.

Testbed and methodology:
- Models: Llama-13B-dense, Mistral-7B-fused, Qwen-14B-long-context-variant, and an MoE-variant (base 7B with 32 experts, 2 experts selected).
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-40GB (primary), NVIDIA H100-80GB for a subset of runs to test kernel scaling.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime nightly branch w/ latest kernel fusion and KV cache prefetch hooks.
- Workloads: synthetic token distributions (uniform, conversational burst, repeating-prefix) and a sampled production trace (anonymized). Key window sizes: 8k, 16k, 32k, 48k, 64k.
- Metrics captured: per-token latency (p50/p95/p99), GPU SM utilization, memory bandwidth, L2/HBM utilization, kernel time breakdown (attention, FFN, router, KV copy), GPU kernel launch counts, and routing imbalance (per-expert token fraction).

Key findings (by architecture):
1) Llama (dense):
- Behavior: linear-ish growth of total latency with token window up to ~32k. After ~48k a second-order effect appears: attention kernel runtime increases more than expected.
- Root cause signal: attention operator switches code path when sequence length crosses internal tiling threshold which increases temporary memory scatters and reduces effective occupancy. We confirmed by instrumenting kernel selection: runs at 48k triggered a fallback path with higher register pressure.
- Observable: SM utilization falls by ~8-12% while memory bandwidth usage rises (more global memory traffic for tiled accumulators).

2) Mistral (fused attention heavy):
- Behavior: efficient at mid lengths (8k-32k) but p95 grows rapidly beyond ~48k.
- Root cause signal: fused attention kernels depend on a single launch that needs workspace proportional to seq_len^2 / tile_factor. At high windows the workspace spills into HBM with extra copies. Also, the fused kernel suffers from bank-contention patterns at particular alignment boundaries observed for our tokenization.
- Observable: sudden jump in kernel runtime; Kernel profiler shows extra device-to-device copies and increased shared memory bank conflicts. H100 mitigates somewhat but does not eliminate because algorithmic workspace remains large.

3) Qwen (long-context variant):
- Behavior: uneven spikes correlated to KV cache miss/eviction events. p99 spikes not strictly monotonic with window size.
- Root cause signal: our KV prefetch policy keeps a fixed working set. Under repetitive-prefix workloads the runtime evicts and reloads KV blocks causing expensive asynchronous copies and kernel reinitialization.
- Observable: elevated PCIe/PCIE-bus-like transfer counters for off-GPU copies in A100; on H100 with NVLink it was less severe but still visible.

4) MoE routing (sparse experts):
- Behavior: mean latency reasonable but p95/p99 explode under skewed routing (hot experts). Even when average per-token work is low, queueing at per-expert buffers creates serialization and kernel re-launch churn.
- Root cause signal: imbalance coupled with small microbatch sizes: when many requests coincide to map to same expert, that expert's kernel sees larger mini-batch and longer runtime while other experts idle; routing control path (host->device enqueues) becomes a bottleneck.
- Observable: per-expert queue depth histograms show long tails; host scheduling latency increased by up to 5x for hot expert launches.

Cross-cutting observations:
- Kernel launch overheads compound for long-context because the number of internal kernel stages grows with sequence length. If combined with small microbatches it shifts runtime from dense compute to kernel-management overhead.
- Memory movement often dominates: temporary workspace bytes scale superlinearly for some fused kernels.
- Tiling thresholds in the compiler/runtime matter. Small changes flip kernel selection and move us from high-throughput to memory-bound code paths.
- MoE variants are sensitive to routing randomness; even balanced global average can hide short-term bursts that dominate tail latency.

Representative numbers (A100, synthetic repeating-prefix workload):
- Llama-13B dense: 32k -> p50 420ms, p95 750ms, p99 1120ms; 64k -> p50 980ms, p95 1.8s, p99 2.5s.
- Mistral-7B fused: 32k -> p50 360ms, p95 700ms, p99 1.1s; 64k -> p50 1.1s, p95 2.2s, p99 3.4s (workspace spill visible).
- Qwen-14B-long: 32k -> p50 480ms, p95 900ms, p99 1.5s (eviction spikes); 64k -> p50 1.3s, p95 2.6s, p99 4.0s (frequent reloads).
- MoE-7Bx32: 32k avg lat 520ms, p95 2.1s, p99 5.2s (hot-expert bursts).

Short experiments that led to root cause confirmation:
- Forced kernel selection toggles: compiling with a lower tiling threshold brought large-window Llama runs back onto high-throughput path and reduced p99 by ~30%.
- Workspace reservation disabled: For Mistral, disabling an optional workspace compaction path eliminated the device-host-device copy at the cost of higher (but contiguous) memory usage and improved p95 by ~25% for 64k runs.
- KV prefetch window sweep: increasing working set size by 1.5x reduced Qwen eviction-induced spikes but increased baseline memory footprint; tradeoff acceptable for dedicated capacity customers.
- Synthetic skew injection to MoE: introducing jitter in routing (probabilistic smoothing) reduced p99 by ~40% but increased average token work ~3%.

Actionable playbook / recommendations:
1) Compile/runtime knobs: tune tiling thresholds per-model family. Add an E2E regression test that runs at 64k tokens during nightly builds to catch path flips.
2) Memory policies: enable configurable workspace reservation for fused kernels to avoid async spill copies when a node is configured with dedicated HBM. Provide a per-deployment knob (low-latency vs low-memory).
3) KV cache heuristics: expose prefetch working-set size and an eviction hysteresis parameter to customers; default to conservative reload-disabled mode for Dedicated tier.
4) MoE routing controls: implement stochastic routing smoothing at the host layer (slight randomization of expert selection on ties) and an emergency backpressure path that switches to a dense fallback model when any expert queue depth exceeds threshold.
5) Microbatch shaping: where latency SLOs matter, prefer slightly larger microbatches to amortize kernel-launch overhead. Add a heuristic that coalesces very small microbatches at the worker side for long-context requests.
6) Observability: add per-expert queue depth metrics, kernel selection logs (tile path id), and a workspace-spill flag in traces. Surface these in Console per-route and tie alerts to p95 regressions.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can compiler-level fusion be modified to produce workspace-bounded kernels for very long contexts (algorithmic research item)?
- Quantization effects: does int8 or q4x better interact with tiled vs fused kernels at long windows? Quick tests indicate small accuracy/latency gains for dense but more unstable patterns for fused kernels. Need a systematic sweep.
- Can we design a lightweight per-request routing oracle that predicts hot-expert risk before scheduling and routes to a dense fallback early?

Appendix (run notes & quick commands):
- repro-sweep.sh: runs synthetic traces at windows=[8k,16k,32k,48k,64k] and collects nvprof/kerneltimes.
- quick-checks: 
  * toggle-tile-threshold: SERVER_FLAG=tile_threshold=8192 ./serve --model llama13b 
  * reserve-workspace: SERVER_FLAG=reserve_workspace=true ./serve --model mistral7b 
  * kv-prefetch: SERVER_FLAG=kv_prefetch_ws=1.5 ./serve --model qwen14b_long 
  * moe-smoothing: SERVER_FLAG=moe_smooth_p=0.05 ./serve --model moe7b32

Concluding notes:
This investigation shows there is no single bottleneck: long-context workloads expose different breaking points across model families (kernel selection boundaries, workspace scaling, cache lifecycle, and routing imbalance). Mitigations require both compilation/runtime knobs and higher-level routing and scheduling heuristics. The proposed playbook contains low-risk runtime flags we can roll to Dedicated clusters and experimental compiler changes for longer-term fixes.

If helpful, I can extract a short one-pager for Product and SRE with immediate rollout recommendations (reserve_workspace defaults and MoE emergency fallback).

-- Aisha
